speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in connection with the lay-offs at automobile plants in Windsor and possible lay-offs elsewhere, in the absence of the Minister of Industry I would direct a question to the Prime Minister. Would he place before the House the general agreement between Canada and the United States with reference to automobiles, free trade in parts and the like?
I see the Minister is now here, so I will redirect my question to the Minister of Industry and tell him it has to do with the arrangement between Canada and the United States with reference to autos and auto parts. Is it a fact, as I am informed was stated yesterday in a committee in Washington, that under the arrangement which has been made between our two countries the big three in the auto industry in Canada will, if the agreement is consummated by its acceptance by the Congress of the United States, build only one model in their Canadian plants for the North American market, a smaller model of automobile than is being built today?
Is it a fact, as was reported to me from Washington, that the result of one small model being built in Canadian plants would adversely affect Canadian suppliers, particularly suppliers of steel and other materials used in cars; and is it a fact that the tool, die and machine industry of Canada would suffer greatly since only one set of tooling dies would be required for the Canadian automobile industry?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: POSSIBLE RESULTS OF CANADA-U.S. AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not had access to the document from which the right hon. gentleman is quoting, but to the best of my knowledge there is not in existence now any plan to limit Canadian production to one small model of one automobile. The motor car manufacturers in Canada are in the process
of endeavouring to make plans to augment, to increase very substantially, their production in Canada. These plans are not yet finalized, but from what I have learned of the progress of the plans to date the intention, as suggested, to limit production in Canada to one small model of automobile is not likely to be the result.

subtopic: POSSIBLE RESULTS OF CANADA-U.S. AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Whether it is likely to be the result or not, has this been discussed as a possible solution of the problem?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: POSSIBLE RESULTS OF CANADA-U.S. AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. As I indicated, this has not been propounded as a possible solution of the problem.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Labour. Would he care to report to the House on his meeting this morning with Mr. Scott, president of Ford of Canada? Did he discuss with him the movement of their purchasing department to head office in Detroit, and did he also discuss with him the reason Ford cars are being sold more cheaply in Buffalo than they are in Canada?

We shall be meeting later in the week, on Thursday, with Mr. George Burt, the international representative of the U.A.W. The purpose of the meeting was to discuss important questions, and the matters raised by the hon. Member were not discussed at this meeting.

I do not recall the exact expression used by my hon. friend, but there is available within the Department of Labour a manpower service which could be utilized to meet a situation of this kind. However, it does involve its voluntary acceptance by both management and labour.
At the present time we are in the process of securing from all the automobile manufacturers information regarding the extent of the manpower adjustments which may be required as a result of the changes with respect to the Ford plant. As I mentioned yesterday there will be temporary lay-offs over a period of time. The expectation is that the lay-offs which will take place in May and June can be met through extending employment opportunities in the Windsor area, and at present the National Employment Service is on the scene and will be available to assist actively, and I trust successfully, the workers displaced from the Ford plant. At present we are in the process of considering what, if any, additional machinery may be required to meet the problem which will affect the workers of higher seniority who may be involved later in the summer. But I would point out that as a result of the discussions held this morning, and placing the problem in its total perspective, the situation is not as serious as the first reaction might have indicated last week.

subtopic: POSSIBLE RESULTS OF CANADA-U.S. AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT

Mr. Speaker, I thought we had dealt with this matter yesterday, but so there can be no question in this regard I should like to simply indicate that well before the accord between the Governments of Quebec and France was executed in February of 1965 three way discussions took place among the officials of the Canadian, French and Quebec Governments with a view to working out a procedure by which the arrangements which Quebec wished to enter into with the competent French authorities could have international effect.
The approach agreed upon on all sides was that the Canadian and French Governments would grant their formal assent to or concurrence in the arrangements, and that this would be done by an exchange of notes between representatives of the Federal Government and of France. The exchange of notes was a type of umbrella agreement between the two Governments under which international effect was given to an arrangement which otherwise would have had no standing in international law.
The agreement was signed by Quebec with France in Paris on February 27. By prearrangement an exchange of notes took place on the same day between the French charge d'affaires here in Ottawa and myself. In this exchange of notes between the representative of France and myself, the Canadian Government concurred in-that is, gave its assent to the agreement between France and Quebec.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF RETIREMENT AGE FOR SENATORS

speechtext:
The House resumed, from Monday, April 26, consideration in Committee of the following resolution-Mr. Mcllraith-Mr. Lamour-eux in the Chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the retirement, upon attaining the age of seventy-five years, of any person appointed to the Senate after the coming into force of the said measure: to extend the provision of the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act to such persons; to provide for the granting of an annuity to any person appointed to the Senate before the coming into force of the said measure who resigns his place in the Senate after having attained the age of seventy-five years or having become afflicted with a permanent infirmity disabling him from the performance of his duties; and to provide further for the granting of an annuity to the widow of a person who was granted such an annuity upon resigning his place in the Senate.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF RETIREMENT AGE FOR SENATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think most Members of the House were very interested to see the resolution on this matter brought
April 27, 1965	COMMONS
before Parliament at this time. It is something that has been in the minds of many Members of this House for a long time, I think, and we are very glad to see that we now have an opportunity to discuss the matter. I think the Government's proposal, as we understand it, is very good as far as it goes; but it does not go very far. In fact, to say it is taking a giant step slowly would be an underestimate as to the length to which this measure will take us. However, Mr. Chairman, even a small step is perhaps better than no step at all.
Since the purpose of the resolution stage, as I understand it, is that the Government may get ideas from Members in all parts of the House on these subjects, I believe now is the time for those of us who are interested in this matter to put forward some of our suggestions. One of the great criticisms of our system of Cabinet Government is that the Prime Minister is so limited in his choice of Cabinet Ministers that a great deal of talent that he might otherwise be able

This would enable the Prime Minister to recommend to His Excellency that perhaps two or three very highly qualified, outstanding Canadians be appointed to the other place, and then the Prime Minister could call them into his Cabinet. Thus we would have some of the advantages of the United States cabinet system in that some of the very ablest people in the country could in effect be called upon by any Prime Minister to serve in his Cabinet. This is something, of course, that the Americans have done, their whole constitutional system being quite different from ours; but they have had this advantage for very many years, and we have not.
If this suggestion were accepted by the Government it would enable the Government to call upon some of the ablest people in Canada to serve with the Government regardless, perhaps, of the political persuasion they might have. For this reason I think the suggestion made yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition-and I noticed that the Prime Minister was paying particular attention to it-should be given much more careful and further consideration by the Government.

As we know, in recent years we have had a number of political parties, other than the two principal ones in the country, which

I believe he went further, not only in this debate but in similar debates-redistribution and the like-and propounded the theory that for every individual there should be one vote, and that democracy should rely entirely upon that basis. I am afraid I cannot agree with the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre in that particular regard.
Let me say that I agree that the principle of elective representation is the main principle which should be considered in setting up any kind of democratic government. But other principles are also involved which have been set forth by those who have studied

political systems from the days of Plato right down to the present time. If you allow a government to be composed of a simple majority, many minorities will be ignored. It is just as easy to have tyranny in a majority government as tyranny in many other ways. For reasons which I have mentioned this is so particularly in Canada, where you have a very large area with different segments forming the country, such as the far western provinces, the Maritime provinces and the two major central provinces. This leads to different political parties forming the provincial governments, each with a different kind of political thinking.
In a country like Canada, for reasons I have already pointed out, due to the way in which our system works in practice it may not be possible to have representation in the other place of those who are not members of the two principal parties; and this has been the case up to the present time. Nevertheless, as long as other political parties do exist in the country, even though they may be on a provincial basis only, it seems only reasonable, if the theory of the Canadian constitution is to work, that they should have representation in the other place.
The only way in which this would be practical at the present time, Mr. Chairman, under the present set-up is through a system of appointments rather than establishing an elective basis. Although it might conceivably be possible to establish some form of electoral basis, since a number of political parties other than the two main ones frequently come into provincial areas it might be better to have some system of provincial political appointments to the other place which would perhaps get around the difficulty which we are facing at the present time.
While the powers of the other place are very great, it is true that in practice they are seldom exercised. Certainly in this century and even during the last century they have been seldom used, but the other place does have a great deal of power of which a lot of people in the country are not aware.

He has attributed to me a reason why this part of the proposed legislation is in the form it is. Perhaps we should discuss the legislation in more detail on the Committee stage of the Bill. What I want to make clear now is that we take the view that those Senators now serving in the Senate were appointed or summoned, I believe the correct word is, under legislation, namely section 29 of the British North America Act, which clearly provided that they would hold their appointments for life. We feel that to take away or change such a right after their appointment, the legislation
April 27, 1965
being in that form, would be a clear infringement of a right which they possess, and we do not wish to do it. It is somewhat analogous to a breach of contract, although perhaps that is not a good analogy to use here. However, it is the same point that arose several times in this Parliament and in the United Kingdom Parliament when attempts were made to change the tenure of office of the judiciary. The better opinion, and certainly the opinion I have always held-although there is one case in Canada where it was not followed by the former Government-is that such an appointment having been made for life, it is wrong arbitrarily to take it away. That being so, we provide a pension which will make it possible for those who wish to retire, having reached the age of 75, to do so. But there is no compulsion on them to retire, because they were appointed with the distinct belief on their part that they were being appointed for life. They had a right to hold that view, because it was and had been provided in the British North America Act for almost 100 years, that they should hold the appointment for life, as distinct from the Members of the House of Commons who have to face elections regularly.
The position is wholly different in so far as persons to be summoned to the Senate in the future are concerned. Of course, I see no difficulty at all in their case; in my view any age limit could be applied to them, or any other limitation as to the expectancy of retaining their position in the Senate. That is the reason the provision is in the Bill. I asked the hon. Member how he would get his Bill passed, because if you once accepted his proposition that the basis on which they were appointed or summoned to the Senate meant nothing, then of course next year we could come along and provide that the age limit be reduced from 75 to 45, which would wipe out a whole group or all of them; or, if the hon. Member should ever have the responsibility of office, he could change the 75 to any other number of years that would effectively wipe out the Senate in this indirect way. That is a principle that I think is quite improper and quite wrong. I hope I have answered the point raised by the hon. Member.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with great interest to the Member for Port Arthur and I take it that his position is the position of the New Democratic Party, who believe the Senate should be abolished. It was once said by the head of the Political Science Department, by the late George Brit-nell, that the only wise Senate that ever existed was the Irish Senate, and they passed a bill to abolish themselves. I do not go as far as the Member for Port Arthur, but there certainly does seem to be a necessity for reform of the Senate. In the few minutes I will take this afternoon, however, I will defend the Senate; I will defend it all the way, because I think it is an important place and performs an important function as far as our Parliamentary institutions in this country are concerned. Certainly the Member for Port Arthur could draw inferences and relate experiences where appointments have been made that probably would have been better left unmade; but that does not mean that the body itself has not a proper function. We should take a look at ourselves in this House if we are to criticize the other place. All of us may not be just as we should be as Members of the House of Commons. We can all throw stones in that regard.
I want to ask this question, Mr. Chairman. As I say, I am defending the Senate, but I am not defending all the Senators in the Senate. My hon. friend from Port Arthur has dealt with that point. However, he did trim his argument at the end of his remarks; he said that if you are not going to abolish the Senate, it should be reformed.
What is the function of the Senate? If you go back you find that it was set up as a union of two distinct cultures and two distinct nationalities at that time; there were minorities, and those minorities had to be protected. There were three important functions. First

of all, the interests of the Provinces had to be protected against legislation passed in this House of Commons; that is, protected other than by the constitution itself. Then it was to protect minorities. Those minorities might at that time have included the Province of Quebec, and at this time includes the Province of Quebec. The Senate is to protect minorities, as I say, and perhaps I may illustrate by giving a hypothetical case. You might have a government elected that left out one section of the country. It might be that a federal government was formed that left out the section of Western Canada entirely. In fact the Liberals were close to that situation; if it had not been for the Minister of Agriculture getting elected in Calgary South they would have had great difficulty in finding a Minister from Alberta and Saskatchewan.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
If something passed the House of Commons which would be detrimental to Western Canada, then it would be an important function of the Senate to protect a minority interest in Western Canada, or for that matter a minority interest in the Province of Quebec or a minority interest in the Maritimes. That is an important function of the Senate. Another function, examples of which many people could draw on from their experience, is to correct the errors and impulses of the House of Commons. They are the three important functions.
Now why, Mr. Chairman, was the Senate devised in that way? There were to be 24 Senators from Upper Canada and 24 Senators from Lower Canada. There were to be 24 from the Maritimes and, after some amendment, 24 were to be appointed from Western Canada. Then an additional six were appointed from Newfoundland, which if my arithmetic is correct brings the number to 102. The membership of the Senate is not based on representation by population but on certain of the localities, and interest in those localities, whether they be economic, social, political or cultural. That is why we have a Senate.
I do not think we can go as far as the original planners had in mind with regard to the Senate. I think it was Sir John A. Macdonald who said, when talking of setting up the Senate and defining its functions:
There would be no use of an Upper House if it did not exercise, when it thought proper, the right of opposing or amending or postponing the legislation of the Lower House. It would be of no value whatever were it a mere chamber for registering

Therefore he might have appointed a Conservative, as Sir John A. Macdonald appointed a Liberal. In other words, Mr. Chairman, the appointments have been political appointments and I do not think that anybody can hide that situation.
I should like to see the Senate reform in this regard, and one of the suggestions made on several occasions and again this afternoon is that the provinces should have something to say in the matter. For example, I think no one has fought the Social Credit party politically in Alberta as much as I have, but a man like the Hon. E. C. Manning, Premier of Alberta, has served for 20 years as Premier of that Province, has a complete knowledge and experience of the petroleum and oil industries, and would be an excellent appointment to the Senate, if he would accept one. Therefore it seems to me that the suggestion that some of these appointments should be made by the Provinces is a good one.
Another suggestion which is being made is that part of that body should be appointed for a set period, and part of it elected. How that should be worked out, a Committee should probably consider, but it does seem strange that once Senators are appointed they are appointed for life, a state of affairs which cannot be changed no matter whether or not they serve their country well. I suggest that we should have a division, with some members elected and some appointed. In particular some should be appointed by the Provinces so that in this way the interests of the provinces are protected. Men who have served their Provinces well and have experience of their localities could serve their country well in their capacity in the Senate.
It is very easy to take extreme examples, as did the hon. Member for Port Arthur today. I was rather amused by this-I mean amused in the right sense-because it is easy to point to one individual and say what he has done, that he may have appeared before a commission and rolled his eyes in a certain way when asked a particular question. But that does not mean that the constitution of the whole body is wrong. We have had good men in the Senate, like Mr. Power and Mr. Meighen, and there are men there today doing a good job. I repeat that their first
fMr. Woolliams.]
job is to protect minorities. If minorities are to be protected in this country and if the Members from the Province of Quebec, who surely are a minority, want to see them preserved, then the protection of those rights is in fact guaranteed by the Senate. I am sure that any Government here, or group of men, would defend the Senate and its function in respect of any legislation passed by a Government which was harmful to a minority, and I am sure that hon. Members here from the Province of Quebec, just like the Members for Western Canada, would support that view.

Certain appointments have been political in nature, which did not really serve the best interests of this country, but that is no reason for doing away with an institution set up for specific purposes and functions.

Mr. Chairman, to complete my remarks, very briefly I should like to touch upon a point raised by my hon. friends to the right, particularly by the hon. Member for Edmonton West, in relation to tyranny of a majority.
Let me say at the outset that there is something of a democratic principle involved. It is my understanding that if a majority which is elected acts in a tyrannical way, the solution or answer within a democratic process, aside from whatever judicial processes may give protection, is to be found at the next election. In a sense the argument the hon. Member has put forward, that the Senate provides protection for minority rights under this kind of a situation against the tyranny of a majority, is in fact a suggestion that we must have something which is not democratic and related to the electors within our system. I personally cannot accept that suggestion.
Perhaps I might now refer to a statement made by-

I would be glad to answer the questions in a moment or two when I have concluded my remarks.
I should again like to refer to the statement made by Sir John A. Macdonald in regard to the Senate's function. This statement was contained in a memorandum prepared for Senator Robertson regarding tha
April 27, 1965
reasons given by a proponent of Confederation for the constituency of a second chamber. The memorandum in part states:
In introducing the motion for approval of the resolutions passed at the Quebec Conference in the House of Assembly, Attorney General Macdonald said, with regard to the proposal to constitute the legislative council:-
I will only read a portion of the quotation as follows:
"When I speak of representation by population, the House will of course understand that universal suffrage is not in any way sanctioned, or admitted by these resolutions, as the basis on which the constitution of the popular branch should rest."
My point really is that Macdonald had a view that did not even envisage the House of Commons as being popularly elected. As my hon. friend knows, there was a limitation on the franchise at that time, and that since the Senate was constituted there have been changes. I do not think any Member here of any party would argue against the idea that on the basis of our Parliamentary system the House of Commons is popular representation by popular choice. This kind of argument by a man who, in a sense, put over Confederation seems to be one more good argument for the fact that the situation has changed. I do not think a minority, with the exception perhaps of large business interests, has ever really been protected by the Senate and I think there are many examples to prove this.
I have in my mind an article which appeared in Maclean's magazine of August, 1961 written by Jean-Luc Pepin, who is, I am sure all hon. Members know, a Liberal Member of Parliament. I think my understanding of the French language is sufficient that I can say with safety that he lists five different sweeping recommendations in regard to Senate reform. As far as he is concerned, apparently the Senate is an accepted institution. One of his proposals relates to a change in the method of choosing Senators in order to reduce the average age. He proposes a number of requirements, including Senate representation in the Cabinet, and Parliamentary Secretaries drawn from the Senate in order to tie that chamber in more effectively. He also suggests, as did the previous speaker, that some of the Members of the Senate should be elected. He was arguing at that time as a political scientist and I should like to quote his last two sentences. I hope my French speaking friends will forgive me for my pronunciation. His last two sentences are these:
Retirement Age for Senators [Translation]
Perhaps then we might see a rehabilitation of the Senate. Otherwise, we would have to insist upon its abolition.

In other words he says that if we cannot attain this kind of reform he favours abolition. Since that individual is a supporter of this Government and very close to the Cabinet, I draw that fact to the attention of hon. Members.
I should like to quote from an article written by Charles Lynch, who I suggest is in many ways our most popular journalist. This article appeared last year in the Ottawa Citizen, and Mr. Lynch said:
Years ago in a bull session, I heard Lester Pearson argue against the case for reforming the Senate.
His view, if memory serves, was that it would be fatal to inject men of youth and vigour into that withered old arm of Parliament because the first thing they would want to do would be to do something.
Inevitably, such Senators would chart a collision course with the House of Commons, and parliamentary paralysis would ensue.
That was long before Mr. Pearson became a party leader in the Commons, much less prime minister-but subsequent events seem to have borne him out. Every time the senators shake their lethargy and start taking their responsibilities seriously, the machinery of Parliament, which is pretty wonky at best, shudders to a stop.
Mr. Lynch was referring to the stand taken last year by Senator Grattan O'Leary, and in the last part of this article he states:
Mr. O'Leary in the Senate reminds us of what might have happened had Field Marshall Viscount Montgomery accepted the governor-generalship of Canada when it was offered him after the war. Fortunately for Monty and the rest of us, he declined when informed that the job carried no power.
Monty would have wanted to whip the country into shape and make something of his office in terms of power-a ghastly thought.
So it is with Senator O'Leary-unless he's kidding,
Mr. Lynch has humorously asked the question whether it is possible to reform the Senate and give it any power without making it a really dangerous institution, making everything haywire. It seems to me that what Mr. Lynch is suggesting is that it should be allowed to go on sleeping. That may be a defensible position.
My suggestion in connection with this legislation is that it is not drastic enough or radical enough to really disturb the Senate's sleep. It is completely inadequate as a reform proposal, particularly coming from a Party which claims to speak for reform.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to conclude my remarks by referring again to this conflict of interest, and I do so at this time to underline the need, if we are going to have reform, for drastic reform. I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail on July 8, 1964, but before doing so let me make it clear that the Globe and Mail does not advocate the abolition of the Senate as I and the Members of my Party do. This article states in part:
The public, which is perhaps more simple and direct in its thought processes than some senators, is likely to be disturbed by what has been happening in the Senate Banking and Commerce Committee.	, . .	.
To put it simply and directly, what has been happening is this: the Committee has been processing private legislation designed to create a number of new banks and mortgage companies. Some of the Senators on the Committee are directors of existing banks to which the new banks would be rivals. Or they are directors of the parent companies of the new mortgage companies. Or they are both.
One of these director-Senators, Senator T. A. Crerar, declared his private interest in the matters before the Committee and withdrew from its deliberations. A number of others, Senator Salter Hayden, chairman of the Committee, Senator P. J. Bouffard, Senator Gordon Isnor, Senator Eric Cook and Senator Hartland de M. Molson, possessed similar private interests, admitted them, but did not withdraw.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The Banking Committee then proceeded to approve the legislation permitting the establishment of the new mortgage companies, which could benefit the companies of which some of the members are directors, but found it necessary to delay the legislation permitting the establishment of the new banks, which would compete with the banks of which some of them are directors.
The Senators gave reasons for what they did, and what they did may have been right. The trouble is that it does not look right.
Senator Hayden defended his action and the action of other director-senators. It would be quite improper as well as illegal, he acknowledged, for a Senator "to vote upon any question in which
IMr. Fisher.1
he has any pecuniary interest whatsoever, not held in common with the rest of the Canadian subjects of the Crown".
This, to the simple and direct minds of those other Canadian subjects, would seem to prevent director-senators of companies interested in establishing new mortgage companies from voting on the subject. Directors get paid.
Senator Hayden's defense of this kind of voting was a little complicated, but he was entirely simple and direct on the matter of Senators who were bank directors voting on banking issues. It would be wrong for a Senator to legislate for his own bank, he explained, but right for him to legislate for the rivals of his bank.
We can look for a vast torrent of explanations from the red chamber to prove that these senatorial activities are all right and proper. But the explanations won't wash. The position of our legislators is like the position of our courts; not only must justice be done it must be seen to be done; not only must legislators avoid conflicts of interest, they must be seen to avoid them.
It is doubtful if directors of banks, mortgage companies, trust companies or any sort of financial institution should sit on the Banking Committee, especially at this time, when the committee will be considering the report of the Porter Royal Commission on Banking and Finance, which could affect all their companies. Their special knowledge of such affairs would not be lost if the Committee were composed entirely of lay Senators; they could always be called, or requested to appear, as expert witnesses.
It is certain that no Senator who has a personal interest, either direct or indirect, in an issue before the Committee should take part in judging that issue. However pure his heart may be, he is still creating in the public mind the suspicion of a conflict of interest. The only course open to him, if he respects the body of which he is a Member and the country it serves, is that taken by Senator Crerar-to declare his interest and withdraw.
This editorial again highlights what is a very real factor in the make-up of the Senate at the present time. In other words, it is eminently a conservative institution, particularly in its active Members, if by "conservative" anyone wants to interpret it as meaning people who represent major financial and corporate interests. I would not want to rule out, Mr. Chairman, the idea of those interests having representation in some ideal forum. However, when such gentlemen tend to dominate a particular institution or when they are able in a sense to perpetuate an interest in financial matters, and these financial interests are added to many times because Senators are so popular as directors of large corporations, then in fact the Senate has lost any real trace of a wide representation of the country. I say this with all due respect to people like Senator Gladstone, Senator Roebuck or Senator Yuzyk, who appear to have been appointed to represent, to a degree, certain special interests.
If we are going to have reform so that Senators represent particular interests, then

we have to have something more explicit than we are being provided with here. Otherwise, the whole matter of reform and a better composition of the Senate is being left again to the prime ministerial prerogative. His performance in the past, as Mr. Newman's article indicates, has been a pretty sad one. It is for Liberals themselves to be concerned with the issue Mr. Newman raises, the fact that the so-called "new politics" of the Prime Minister have been revealed in terms of Senate appointments as being a pretty shoddy business. This is for the Liberals themselves to settle.
I should like to suggest to the Liberals, in terms of forming some kind of reform of the Senate, that they must come forward with something more than this if they are really going to convince us that they want to use the Senate for other than a place to put party hacks or party bagmen who have collected funds for the party.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to add but a few remarks to those which have already been made on this resolution.
In the first place, the age of a senator or of a candidate to the Senate should not be the main consideration. The measure before this committee seems to attach the greatest importance to age itself, by facilitating the retirement of senators on attaining the age of 75 and even compelling them to retire at that age.
In support of this statement, I will refer to the opinion of a universally recognized authority in this matter, namely Dr. Wilder Penfield, who stated that often a person could render his best contribution in the later part of his life and that it was advantageous for a man or a woman of a certain age to change his or her career and direct his or her activities toward other fields of action.
Therefore, it seems to me that not age but rather the senator's ability to perform his duties ought to be the determining factor. As we all know, some people are already burnt out at 45, while others are still in full possession of their faculties at 75 or even at a more advanced age and their long experience makes them especially useful to the community and the nation and quite capable of filling a Senate appointment.
Incidentally, I have in mind a perfect example to illustrate how a man's career can be usefully extended. I refer to Dr. Penfield, whose appointment to a reformed Senate would be an excellent one.
As for the Senate reform itself, I think everybody agrees that it must be done. Of course, there are those who advocate the abolition pure and simple of the Senate. Others ask for a reform, but even there, opinions are divided. I am not in favour of the abolition of the other place because I feel it plays a useful role. Indeed, parliament does not have unilateral jurisdiction to abolish the Senate.
As someone pointed out, the Senate was established partly to protect the rights of minorities, of the provinces and of particular areas. Representation in the Senate is much more vital to the provinces themselves and if

April 27, 1965

Retirement Age for Senators parliament moves to abolish the other place, it will have to consult the provinces beforehand. I am surely in favour of a reform which would go much deeper than the timid proposal under consideration here.
In my opinion, the reform should be twofold. First, it should concern the choice of appointees to the Senate and, second, it should deal with the duties which the Senate must or should carry out.
With regard to the appointment of Senators, several of the reforms suggested could be considered. First of all, in resorting to the present method of appointment by the government, the Prime Minister should use better judgment. The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) opened old sores by reviewing the appointments to the Senate made by the present Government. Much better judgment should be used than has been the case up to now and it is especially important that the choice should not be based solely on the political credit of a candidate to this office. Yet, this has been undoubtedly and precisely the case up to now with regard to the twenty or so appointments to the Senate made since 1963.
It is useless, I believe, to propose a broadening of the duties of the Senate as long as the methods of appointing Senators are not changed. It is imperative for the Government when making its decision to be more discerning, to select candidates known for their competence in various segments of public and even private life, apart from any other consideration.
I would be in favour of the appointment of candidates as qualified as Mr. Robert Fowler and Mr. Marcel Faribault; they would make very good senators. This reform in the very set-up of the Senate could take place as of now. However, it is necessary to consider more substantial reforms by changing the pattern followed for those appointments. In fact I think that the matter of appointment of Senators should be left to an independent committee. It might be said that such a committee could not be really independent and that it would still remain, to a certain extent, under the Government's thumb. That may be true, but as far as redistribution is concerned, Commissions have been appointed and they are performing their duties in an unbiased way. As far as I know, no pressure has been exercised on the Commissions either by the house or the government. An independent commission could do this work just as impartially and select the best qualified candidates.
With regard to the reform of the Senate, making that body elective could also be considered. I think that in the long run it would be the best way of ensuring that a candidate has the necessary qualifications to perform his duties. I would therefore suggest, if we choose to proceed by way of constitutional amendment, that Senators be selected on an elective and province-wide basis. In other words, a certain number of candidates would be proposed for each Province and the electorate would then choose the Senate representatives for the whole province at the time a general election is held on a province-wide basis, without regard for the boundaries of the various ridings. An independent commission, after consultation with the provincial authorities, could establish a slate of candidates for each Province, and Senators would be selected from that slate by the voters. Highly qualified candidates would thus be chosen and at the same time, this would remove the blot on the democratic principle caused by a non-elective body, invested with the authority to suspend the legislative power of Parliament.
In addition to amending the method used to select candidates, it would be advisable to amend drastically the functions that this reformed Senate would be called to fulfil. In my opinion, what that house could do best would be the work of a constitutional committee. I would very much like a Senate made up of the best authorities in Canada hearing evidence throughout the country on those constitutional matters. That would be giving the Senate a very useful role, worthy of that body, in short a role it could play in all respects.
Thus that constitutional committee, made up of all the appointed senators, could sit the same number of days as the House of Commons, and we would no longer see the Senate idle during long weeks, even months, when the House of Commons is engaged in a never ending debate.
I suggest that the government pay serious consideration to those suggested reforms of the Senate, respecting appointments as well as the duties to be fulfilled by that body. The discussion on this resolution could even be postponed until the government has had the opportunity of bringing drastic reforms within the Senate.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that this measure is too vague to reach the objective which was set, and in my opinion, the government should postpone it and introduce a better drafted and more useful motion or resolution.

Some people can carry themselves out of the chamber. They are preparing themselves for the Senate. They are getting used to sitting on their seats without doing anything.
The operations of Parliament have become a common topic across the nation; people are looking at it in terms of Parliament as a whole, the Senate as well as the House of Commons. I think the Government has accepted this by suggesting that some modification be made in the arrangements pertaining to the other place. It is interesting to note that there is a similarity of opinion among many Members of this House with regard to the operations of the Senate, and I believe this opinion is shared by many of the citizens of this country. There are large numbers of Canadians, in fact, who feel that the whole institution of Parliament including both Houses has got itself into serious disrepute. I believe everyone who considers the question of the Senate does so in the terms of what he or she wishes to see accomplished by that institution. It is a fact that Parliament is divided into these two parts. This is because we have inherited our institutions from the Mother Parliament, a parliamentary system which involves a House of Lords. There are those-and some of them are very close to me in this chamber-who would agree that the establishment in Canada of a House of Lords in its entirety would be a good thing. I am sure there are many in Canada who would not disagree with the idea of hereditary titles. I notice that the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre laughs; he thinks he might be called Lord Winnipeg or something like that. However, I think it would be an advantage to have attached to us an august body which would avoid many of the pitfalls which are present today. There are those who say a man can be born into a certain role. Certainly this is true in the case of many of our financial institutions and large corporations where sons follow their fathers, for no good reason except that they have been left considerable fortunes and money seems to make money. If we had a House of Lords in Canada and titles were hereditary, no longer would Prime Ministers be able to appoint to the other place politicians or others whose only qualifications were services rendered, services
Retirement Age for Senators which had to be rewarded. Listen to the argument. Many people in Canada support the idea that religious bodies should be represented in the Senate, and that these representatives should be appointed by the churches themselves rather than by the party in power. Well, in Great Britain when a clergyman reaches the rank of bishop he becomes automatically a member of the House of Lords.
I know there are judges in this country, even if they were politically appointed, without proper qualifications for the job, many of them political hacks in the first place lacking even legal training-I know many of them would feel it appropriate if senior judges were automatically made Members of the Upper Chamber as is the case in England. This might be a new approach to the correction of some of the ills of the Senate as it is presently constituted. If we were to apply the English system with automatic appointments from the bench and from the ranks of the ecclesiastical authorities we might do better in having broad-minded and reasonable people in the other place than is the case at the present time when Senate seats are used to reward those who have raised a great deal of money for a political party, and so on, with the result that the Upper Chamber has become a haven for retired politicians.
It may be wise, then, to give consideration to the British system, its development and its application. For my part I believe the Government is being unfair in what it is doing at the present time. I say this because I have an arch-enemy in the Senate in Senator Roebuck. I think he is a very good man who is opposed to social changes, many of which I favour. I would be the first to say that although he has lived for more than 80 years he has not lost any of his ability. Indeed, in my opinion he is far superior to many of those much younger than he is, who sit in this House or in the other chamber. I hope that when I reach the age of retirement I will have the good health and the mental capabilities that Mr. Roebuck enjoys. If we pass this measure we are saying to Senator Roebuck: You no longer have a contribution to make. I think this would be stupid, particularly when there are others who, as my hon. friend from Port Arthur has said, had no capabilities in the beginning and will never have anything to give to the Canadian people. Though I may disagree with aspects of the proposal which
April 27, 1965

Retirement Age for Senators Senator Roebuck has made, I must acknowledge they have been worth-while and capably executed.
I am sure that age is not a satisfactory criterion of ability, and this is borne out by the records of some of our judges. If the Senate is intended to provide the opportunity to take a second, sober look at things, what we need in that institution is some thought of any description, and those who are capable of providing it should be given an opportunity of doing so. Some of those in the Senate who are over 80 years of age are attending their duties regularly. Why change the situation? I think the general public is well aware that many of the Senators are carried into that institution to fulfil the requirement which says they have to make an annual appearance or lose their right to sit and receive indemnities. We used to see this practised in the mines. We used to see miners brought there in casts, and held there so that they would not be able to obtain compensation. No one thought these miners carried in on stretchers were there for the purpose of mining. The only reason they were brought there was so the mine did not have to pay a penalty to the Compensation Board. I think perhaps this is what happens to some of the Senators that we have; if they were to be retired they would have to be kept by the political party which put them there, and the party is not prepared to do this.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
The people of Canada are interested in our parliamentary institutions. They certainly are interested in the House of Commons, and I think we do not really have to say much about that because the Canadian public are going to do it for us. I think they will also look at the Senate and wonder why the Senate has not been able to eliminate some of the things which they think are wrong with this particular institution. I believe when they do this they will wonder about the method of appointment, and what this is for. We are all aware of the system that is used at the present time. We know that this is a retirement place for tired politicians, for defeated candidates, for others who have not been able to make the grade in the political field but have filled war chests of the political party which they support. I think it is safe to say that pretty nearly every Member of the House of Commons will be able to enumerate those Members of the Senate who have not been ap-

pointed on that basis. Let me say that there have been some who were not, but I think it is generally known by the Canadian people that the majority of the Senators were appointed on that basis. I believe this means that the Canadian public are interested and should have some say in what happens in any change in or reform of that institution.
We could make the Senate an elected body. I think that if you took this proposal as a referendum to the Canadian people, they would be opposed to it. I believe they would be opposed to it for the same reason they are upset about the operation of the House of Commons. They have one elected body that is not doing very well, so why get another? The general public would, I think, make short shrift of the idea of electing a second body. There is a third way in which appointments could be made to the Senate. It seems to me these could be made by the provinces. I really wonder whether the Liberal Government has given any consideration to this, because are the Provinces not running this Government at the present time? We have no leadership in Ottawa today. The Liberal Party is not giving it; it is going to the Provinces. Every time it has a major proposal to make, it goes to the Provinces and has a conference. We have had more Dominion-Provincial Conferences in the last few years than we have ever had before.

It is not that we want people in the Senate, because if we had wanted them the offer has been made on several occasions and could have been taken advantage of; but we did not want representation in the Senate. Mr. Chairman, may I make a comment of two or three minutes duration. Since I spoke yesterday I have listened with great interest to various remarks which have been made, noting particularly that no Member from the Liberal Party has had anything to say about the resolution before us, excepting the sponsor who spoke briefly. Nevertheless there has been expressed a variety of suggestions about ways to reform the Senate. We in this Party are fairly clear

about our attitude toward the Senate, that it is not possible to reform it and that it should be abolished. But these other divergent views really reflect what people at home are perhaps thinking, and have been thinking for many years, about the Senate.
The suggestion has been made that the Senate might be an elected body entirely. There has been the suggestion that perhaps part of it be elected and part appointed. There has been the suggestion that it should be appointed to represent a particular economic or social interest in the nation. It has been suggested that it should be given certain work to perform, that Bills should be introduced there, that they should have Parliamentary Secretaries and that Senators should be members of the Cabinet. There have been a variety of suggestions which basically seek to make changes in the operation of the Senate so that it will become a useful and functioning unit within the parliamentary system. We have even had reference to articles written by Members of Parliament who are silent or absent at the moment. One Jean-Luc Pepin was referred to, as was John Napier Turner, who is probably on his way to Russia at the moment, or at least getting ready for the trip. They also wrote articles about the Senate, pretty stringent articles, and each came to the conclusion that the only way out was to abolish this useless and expensive appendage.
What I wish to suggest to the President of the Privy Council, who introduced the resolution and will probably be piloting the Bill through the House, if his activity at this stage is any indication, is that the Bill is a proper subject for study by a Committee of the House. In this way the divergent views which have been expressed here, and the views of anyone else in the Upper Chamber interested in either reform or abolition of the Senate, may be made known so that the entire subject matter can be dealt with at great length. Then when the Committee reports to the House it will have the benefit of discovering the attitude of Canadians from all walks of life in regard to the Senate. Then out of that course of action, even though our position is that the Senate should be abolished, there may be some meat which will help make the Senate a useful and functioning body within our parliamentary system.
Even though I would seek to abolish the Senate, because I really think it serves no useful purpose in society, except for the Cana-
April 27, 1965

dian taxpayer who pays the salary of Senators to enable them to go around and collect campaign funds for the party in office, I still recognize the fact that the Senate will not be abolished today or indeed in this session of Parliament. In fact, it will not be abolished for a long time to come, if ever, because regardless of which party may be in office, whether the Liberal Party or the Party to which I belong, we will still need the consent of the Senate to its own abolition, which looks like a pretty formidable obstacle to overcome.
Therefore I would suggest to the President of the Privy Council that he might be well advised to consider establishing a Committee. I do not know whether I would go so far as to suggest a joint Senate-House of Commons Committee because there might be some biased members on it if that course were taken. But if broad terms of reference were given to the Committee to examine the whole structure and functioning of the Senate in the hope that some report might be made to the House and subsequent legislation introduced which would be really worth while, that would perhaps be preferable to introducing a simple, insipid measure such as this, which attempts to retire Senators in the future at 75 years of age. I toss this suggestion out now before the debate concludes, which might be within half an hour, so that perhaps the President of the Privy Council could give an off-the-cuff answer to this proposal, and before second reading might be able to take some deliberative action to get this incisive study under way.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN ADVANCES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, hon. Members will recall that during the last session the National Housing Act was amended in several respects. Considerably more flexibility was introduced to increase the possibilities of housing for low income families, as well as for persons with special housing problems, including elderly people and people in other deserving categories. Urban renewal provisions were introduced to encourage not only conservation but rehabilitation of our cities and other urban communities. The earlier provisions of the Act for the clearance of slums and the redevelopment of such lands were extensively broadened.
It will be recalled also, I am sure, that in the course of the debate in May and June of last year, in response to requests that came from all parts of the House, I made a very positive statement and gave the assurance that we would embark immediately-by "we" I meant the officials of Central Mortgage and myself as the responsible Minister-would embark upon an educational program to ensure a wide and thorough understanding of the amendments that were passed in June last, more particularly an understanding on the part of municipal leaders.
Since these amendments became law in June, I have visited eight of the ten Provinces. I have spent a great deal of time in these Provinces discussing the more detailed aspects of the new legislation with provincial Governments and their officials and, in conjunction with the officials of the Provinces, with representatives of the various Municipalities. I was accompanied on these visits by the President and other senior officials of Central Mortgage and Housing. I think it can be fairly said that we worked as a team with a view to ensuring the widest possible knowledge and a thorough understanding of the said amendments and their possibilities.
Frankly, Mr Chairman, I have been more than pleased, I have been greatly encouraged, by the co-operation we have received from all the Provinces in which these conferences or symposia have taken place. I have been greatly encouraged also by the enthusiasm and interest that have been shown by Mayors, Reeves, Municipal Councillors and other Municipal leaders, and people who have been interested in housing and in urban renewal, in all parts of Canada. Actually, while we
April 27, 1965

visited eight Provinces, we had conferences in only six.
We started off in September in the Province of Nova Scotia. I think all Members who attended, and there were several Members of this House present, will agree that it was a very successful meeting. Premier Stanfield and his Cabinet colleagues joined wholeheartedly in the educational program in which we were engaged and we had two very useful days in Nova Scotia. Since the press communique that was released on that occasion is typical of communiques that were released in the other Provinces since that date, it might be well to read it to the Committee. This is the communique that was issued by the responsible provincial Minister and myself:
The discussions, which ranged over a wide variety of housing and related matters, were highly successful and provided new evidence of the need for a continuing and spirited attack on urban blight and the provision of low cost housing. They revealed, too, an enthusiastic response to the new legislation, and the steadfast intention of the Government of the Province of Nova Scotia and its municipal authorities to avail themselves to the fullest possible extent of the federal aids now afforded and to prosecute fully their efforts to resolve the vexing problems confronting them.
It was only a matter of weeks from the conclusion of that conference in Halifax when we received an application for an urban renewal study from the City of Glace Bay, which has since been acted upon. Others have come in from Nova Scotia. Within a week or so of the Nova Scotia conference, we were in Newfoundland. Indicative of the interest that was aroused at that time, the dynamic and enthusiastic Premier of that Province, Mr. Smallwood, and several Members of his Cabinet, together with the representatives of the Municipalities on the Island of Newfoundland and in Labrador, spent two full, two busy days with us. We now have a fairly complete survey of some areas, but in addition we have positive evidence of the success of the visit in that we have approved applications for urban renewal from St. John's, and other parts of the Island.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
In November, the Minister of Municipal Affairs of the Province of Alberta and I were invited by the Union of Municipalities of that Province to attend their annual session in Lethbridge. I was accompanied by the President and other senior officials of C.M.H.C., and I think it was a most fortuitous arrangement because we had the Mayors and senior officials of almost every
National Housing Act
municipality in Alberta present on that occasion. It afforded a wonderful opportunity for us to outline and explain the possibilities of the new legislation. I am very grateful to the executive of the Union of Municipalities of Alberta for their kind and timely invitation.
Shortly before Christmas we were in Toronto and several Members of the House from three or four of the parties were present on that occasion. We had representatives there totalling some 600 people from Southern and Eastern Ontario. This was followed by a meeting in January, in Vancouver, of the municipal and provincial leaders of the Province, representing the government and the cities and towns of B.C. Then, in the latter part of January we had a further meeting at Sault Ste. Marie where the provincial Ministers concerned were joint hosts with the Federal Government. The meeting was attended by representatives of most of the towns and cities of Western and Northern Ontario.
I am pleased to announce that another symposium of the same nature will be held in Charlottetown on May 8, still another in Fredericton, New Brunswick on May 10, and on May 29 there will be a similar one at Winnipeg, and on May 31 at Regina. These will round out visits to all the Provinces.
In every case the Provincial Governments have joined with the Federal Government in invitations to the Municipalities to attend, and they have participated enthusiastically in the discussions, which I feel have been very fruitful. I might add that following each and every one of the conferences that have been held we have conducted intensive education programs in conjunction with the provincial authorities, with a view to educating, or perhaps passing on would be a better term, to the Municipalities information regarding the possibilities of the new legislation.
The response of the Provinces, in the form of provincial legislation to implement the legislation that this Parliament passed in June last, has been timely. Legislation has now been passed in Alberta, in Saskatchewan and in Manitoba it is before the respective Legislatures. In fact, the Manitoba Bill may have gone through today.
Similar legislation was passed last year in Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. In Ontario, the Ontario Housing Corporation has come into being and it has done a magnificent job in the eight or nine months that

April 27, 1965
National Housing Act
have elapsed since their complimentary legislation was passed.
By the end of last month, as a result at least to some extent of this educational program and other educational moves that have been taken, Federal contributions were requested and granted for a total of 60 urban renewal studies. That is the initial step which leads to a program of area development, rehabilitation and conservation in our cities, and I think the groundwork is now being laid that will show that a nationwide campaign is under way to reclaim and modernize vast sections of our towns and cities. I am sure hon. Members will appreciate the potential impact of this demand that is coming from all ten Provinces for Federal financial assistance.
Grants for the preparation of definite urban renewal schemes, first provided for in last summer's amendments, have already been made for ten renewal projects. These proposals range from a five-acre scheme to improve traffic conditions in Burnaby, B.C. to a vast 1,000 acre renewal undertaking planned for the City of Hamilton. I might say I think the Hamilton scheme is the most imaginative, most comprehensive and most carefully thought out of any brought to my attention during the past year. Other centres currently preparing renewal schemes include Moncton, St. John's, Sudbury, Trois Rivieres, Windsor and Vancouver.
Since June last, the Federal Government has also undertaken to assist two municipalities in the implementation of schemes actually approved earlier. The first involves a contribution of $4.4 million to Hamilton to acquire and clear some 30 acres of land in an over-all renewal project of some 270 acres in the north end of that city. Through this form of assistance the Federal Government will share as well the cost of undertaking an extensive municipal works and services program that must complement the urban renewal scheme. The second grant, which is approximately $2 million, will enable Vancouver to acquire and clear 28.5 acres in three separate renewal projects in the east end of the downtown section of the city, partly in the riding of my hon. friend from Vancouver East. Grants for the servicing of renewal projects undertaken earlier in Kingston and Ottawa have also been authorized.
As you are aware, Mr. Chairman, last summer's revision of the Act also introduced new and substantial assistance to aid Provinces and Municipalities which wish to undertake public housing for low income families and

individuals. As an alternative to the usual joint Federal-Provincial partnership arrangements for such projects, Provinces and Municipalities are now offered long-term loans equal to 90 per cent of the costs involved for this type of development.
This new form of Federal aid has attracted wide attention throughout the whole of Canada, but especially in Ontario where their new Housing Corporation has embarked upon an ambitious program aimed at providing a minimum of 12,000 loan-assisted public housing units within the next three years. This Provincial Corporation is now engaged in evaluating the need for this type of accommodation in Municipalities throughout Ontario. Discussions have already commenced with officials of Metropolitan Toronto and 37 other communities for approximately 4,500 units. As provided in last year's amendments, the Federal Government has also undertaken in each case to meet one half of any losses sustained in the operation of these public housing projects.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
While this new program gives promise of making a substantial contribution to the supply of sorely needed public housing accommodation in Canada, the past nine months have also seen an upswing in the number of projects authorized for development under Federal-Provincial partnership arrangements, which have been in force for some little time. During this period agreements have been signed for eight such projects, which will provide a total of 1,031 units and require an investment of approximately $10.5 million of Federal funds. Two developments approved for Vancouver will consist of a total of 564 units, while 211 dwellings are proposed for St. John's and 184 for Halifax. The remaining four projects will be in Kingston, Hamilton, Oshawa and Swift Current. Augmenting the increasing volume of public housing activities there has been marked interest in the new provisions of the Act authorizing 90 per cent loans to non-profit corporations for low-rental accommodation. These loans can be used for the construction of dormitories and hostels as well as for self-contained family units.
There is another aspect of last year's amendment to which I wish to refer. Hon. Members will recall the aid given for housing on university campuses. Each year has seen increasing demands made for Federal assistance for university housing projects. In 1964 alone, loans amounting to almost $40 million
April 27, 1965

were authorized for projects accommodating some 7,200 students. A further $10 million was committed in the first three months of this year and new proposals have been received by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for projects involving an additional $5 million.
Since the inception of this program only four years ago, Federal funds in excess of $120 million have been extended under the Act for 103 university housing projects which will provide on-campus accommodation for more than 24,000 resident students. I hope Members of the Committee will agree that we have not been inactive-when I say "we" I am referring mainly to the efficient and dedicated officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation-in our efforts to ensure that the provisions of the National Housing Act are fully and thoroughly understood and implemented in the way this Parliament intended when it passed the amendments.
With this statement as background and in view of the fact that so many provinces and municipalities have already evinced an interest to the point of taking action, it is readily apparent why the present resolution is now before this committee. As for residential construction, in the past year it reached a level never before recorded in Canada. The figure of 165,658 housing starts financed from all sources was 11.5 per cent higher than the previous year. There were 150,963 dwelling units completed in 1964, surpassing by almost 18 per cent the number in 1963, and at year end there were 107,718 units under construction. All three of these figures were greater than those in the previous record year of 1958. Under the National Housing Act overall lending activity in 1964 covered 55,640 units. Of these units, 28,681 involved direct loans made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Most of the direct loans were in support of the Winter House Building Incentive Program which, Mr. Chairman, has been eminently successful in providing increased winter employment for the building trades-

Mr. Chairman, first I would like to thank the Minister for giving us the review of last year's operations of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation; then I would go on to point out that no Act of recent years has ever been put on the statute books, in my opinion, that has accomplished more, with the support of all parties, than the National Housing Act. In the ten years this Act has been in existence it has been amended eight times, twice by the Liberal Party and six times by the Progressive Conservative Party. This Act has been used by both parties in the Federal Government to take a part in the economy of Canada which I do not think could be matched by Provinces working entirely by themselves. This Act is one of the classic examples of why the initiative in the economic field should never be lost by the Federal Government, because no Act, as I said earlier, has achieved as much as this one.
I would like to point out in passing that during the period we were in office we faced two recessions. I would suggest that of all the measures that we put into effect, whether it was loans to farmers, loans to small businessmen, export credits, tremendous programs of public works, etc., none achieved the results equal to the work that was done under the National Housing Act. I cannot give the Committee the precise number of billions of dollars that we used during that period, but I can remind the Committee that the construction industry is one of the most important and one of the most sensitive that we have in Canada in affecting the national economic health. I think the Act, being passed in 1954, amended in 1956, six times in the years we were in power, and then again last year, is indicative of the fact that we are still learning how to use this Act. The report of the Minister of how he has visited most of the Provinces and carried the knowledge of what this Act can do to not only the provincial representatives but the representatives of Municipalities and organizations is a very important part of the work that should be done under this Act.
In passing, Mr. Chairman, I would like to pay tribute to the late Stewart Bates, who served under Ministers like Hon. Bob Winters, Hon. John Garland, Hon. Howard Green, Hon. David Walker and Hon. Davie Fulton, as well as the present incumbent. I think the Minister would share
April 27, 1965

with me the feeling that the work of Stewart Bates and all those around him has helped Governments, regardless of which party was in power, tremendously in the carrying forward of the administration of this very important legislation.
