speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not going to deal at great length with the actual, precise work that has been done under each section of the Act, but I am going to say at the beginning that I do not believe anyone in the House will be in opposition to the resolution before us this evening to make available to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation the amount of money necessary to do the jobs laid down under the eight sections of the Act. However, I do want to point out to the Minister some of the feeling of the Opposition Party called Progressive Conservative. We have been looking at this legislation, and we know the legislation has to be constantly changed to meet the rapidly changing conditions. I would like to put before the Minister on behalf of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition four or five suggestions which might be of value to him in discussing the changes that can still be made in future amendments to the legislation.
Regardless of how much good this Act has done, we must face up to the fact that there are still gaps that remain unfilled. It is to these gaps that I wish to direct my attention. The first gap to be filled is in regard to what can be called substandard housing. I know that under the Act this can be dealt with under the public housing section or under the home improvement section; but I would suggest that in this field of substandard housing, which can be described as housing which is going downhill, there is an area where much more can be done. There is a reluctance on the part of the Federal Government, I know, to move any stronger into this field because it has connotations which are provincial. To keep the record reasonably clear I would like to take the liberty of putting on the record one or two clippings from the press that were published after these conferences which the Minister attended. The first one will be from the Toronto Star of December 18, 1964. I will read these quickly to show that this problem is a real one. This article was written by a staff writer, who says:
The Federal Government will consider legislation to make home improvement loans available for major renovation of existing dwellings in its next
National Housing Act
round of amendments to the National Housing Act.
This is the next paragraph, which goes on to say:
Postmaster General John R. Nicholson offered the possibility to a joint federal-provincial symposium on planning, public housing and urban renewal here yesterday.
But he said the Provinces would have to express the desire for an extension of home improvement assistance, the ultimate responsibility for housing being a provincial and municipal affair.
For all our talk and efforts, nearly 100,000 Canadian families live under housing conditions that are appalling-a disgrace to the communities they live in, he said.
Then quoting the Minister:
"They cannot find other accommodation on the open market at rents they can afford, and 20 per cent of all dwellings have "very primitive bathing and toilet facilities'*.
He listed redevelopment, rehabilitation and conservation as the means of halting this "despair".
On the same date in the Globe and Mail I read this, also written by one of their staff writers:
Postmaster General J. R. Nicholson, the Federal Minister responsible for housing matters, made it clear during a symposium that ended in Toronto yesterday that he opposes extending National Housing Act loans to all houses.
N.H.A. loans are available on existing houses in urban renewal areas. Although the house-building industry and real estate boards have been urging governments for years to make N.H.A. loans available on all houses, Mr. Nicholson said at a press conference that he could not support such a step.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
The argument in favour of N.H.A. lending on existing houses has been that it would encourage purchase and rehabilitation of many houses in areas where blight is beginning but can still be checked.
I read those quotations from the two Toronto dailies to show the confusion which can arise in the minds of writers covering the same event.
I now read from a local paper, the Ottawa Citizen for December 26, an editorial which appeared on that day:
There will be broad dissatisfaction over the statement by Postmaster General J. R. Nicholson, the Federal Minister responsible for housing matters, that he is opposed to the extension of National Housing Act mortgages to all houses.
N.H.A. amendments now being implemented are certainly a step in the right direction. They provide for loans, guaranteed by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, on the purchase of older houses in designated urban renewal areas. But N.H.A. mortgage provisions still do not cover the purchase of existing homes on a general basis.
Mr. Nicholson said that action to permit loans on existing houses might be opposed by the Provinces, which have the power to reject N.H.A. amendments in this field. But it would be interesting to learn what steps if any, the Minister

April 27, 1965
National Housing Act
has taken to determine the views of provincial leaders on this matter.
Then, missing a paragraph, the article continues:
Mr. Nicholson has placed emphasis on the needs to rehabilitate the older parts of cities-and understandably so. A move by the federal government to permit N.H.A. mortgages on the purchase of all existing homes would do much to serve this end. At present, development is encouraged in the suburbs rather than in urban areas because of the location of vacant land. Couples unable to make the high down payments required on new homes could buy older houses in the downtown areas if the right N.H.A. amendments were made. These same people could be expected to make improvements to their properties.
I quote those two articles and the editorial, Mr. Chairman, not to contradict what the Minister has said but to show that there is still a gap to be tilled. I do have another clipping from the Globe and Mail which deals with the same subject, but I do not think it adds anything to what I have said.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that this is one gap to fill which may require not only amendment perhaps of the National Housing Act but even greater education, direction and persuasion of the provincial Governments to enable them to take action in this field. Because many of us know from personal experience that there are large areas in our urban centres where it would be better economics to repair houses and build them up to modern standards than to move the people living there into suburban areas, trying to relocate them in that way. This has been the experience of many cities in North America. One of the classic examples to be found is Pittsburgh, not very far away from the area where this symposium was held. In Pittsburgh a good deal of attention was given to the rebuilding of older homes, thereby putting an end to substandard conditions, as a cheaper and more economical way of dealing with the question of housing in large cities.
The second gap, which is very noticeable, in housing legislation in Canada is that there is no provision for those people who want to upgrade their homes. Upgrading can be defined in various ways. A classic example is the case of the young couple who buy a home with two bedrooms with the expectation that they will be able to live in it for 20, 25 or 30 years until their children grow up. But their plans do not quite turn out as they expect and a few years later, after they have started paying off their mortgage and building their environment around this particular home, 
they find children have come along and they require a four bedroom house.
When such a family has to move to a four bedroom type of accommodation they are caught in two ways. First of all, what are they going to do about the equity which they have built up in their home? How do they get rid of the mortgage they already have on the home? Second, they have to accomplish this within some reasonable period in order to be able to start building their new home. I could dwell on this point for some time, Mr. Chairman, but I think I have made my point, which is that this is a gap which does exist so far as the needs of our people in the cities are concerned.
A similar, related type of problem is where a family has to move from one city to another because the firm who hires the husband has transferred him. Once again the husband is up against two difficulties, one of getting his equity out of his original home and getting started on paying for the second home; and there is the difficulty that he incurs real estate fees in getting rid of his first home and more real estate fees in buying the new one. This imposes a heavy burden on any person transferred in such a situation, or who is required to move from a two bedroom house to a four bedroom house. I suggest to the Minister that this is a gap which it would not be too difficult to meet. There are precedents in regard to the question of resale of house mortgages, and so on. As far as I can discover from the Act this particular difficulty is not provided for.
The third gap in the legislation is in the matter of urban renewal, which is probably the most exciting part of the new legislation. I know that when we were in office we put in the sections which provided money for cities to look at the problem, study it and begin to work out a plan. We also got ready to move the amendments which the Minister had the honour to move last year, so there is no question of not being willing to move with the times. My contribution to the debate on the matter of urban renewal will be on a wider scale, I think.
I am not quarreling with what the Minister and his officials are doing in this legislation; I think it is good. But I do think that the officials themselves sense, and as I read the words of the report issued last year they know that there is something wider which must be done. Urban renewal is not a matter of just clearing out worn-out parts of a city and rebuilding them with either residential housing or industrial plants or
April 27, 1965

providing park areas. Urban renewal must be part of an over-all plan for a community. This is dealt with in one sentence of the report, and I think the idea has to be extended so as to tie it in with metropolitan planning. [DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
The day is over when any city thinks it can set up a parks board to plan parks; that a city can set up a transportation committee to plan transportation in the city; that it can set up a body to deal with education and plan for new schools; that it can set up another committee to deal with social welfare services and to provide all the other things necessary in a city. The whole planning operations of cities must be brought together into a co-ordinated activity. We must look ahead, not just for two or three years but for decades. If a city of 500,000 people is involved the citizens must visualize this city as one of a million, a million and a half or two million people. They must visualize the responsibility which they have for that area, and in addition the responsibilities they have in respect of the surrounding areas which depend upon that city. They must consider these responsibilities as well as their own direct constitutional responsibilities within their own boundaries.
Mr. Chairman, that is the concept of modern metropolitan trends which now occupies the thoughts of leaders in North America. The proof of that statement lies in the fact that during the past five years three universities in the United States have established urban sections to their post graduate programs. These graduate sections are concentrating on problems of urban living and development. The first thing they have found is that any city in the course of developing from 100,000 to 500,000 people, or from 500,000 to 1,000,000 people, or from 1,000,000 people to 2,000,000 people makes exactly the same mistake as other cities have made which have gone through these same growth stages.
As a result of the studies made by these graduate schools in the United States, we are beginning to learn that one of the greatest wastes of a modern industrial state is not the result of planning on the part of the Federal-Provincial Governments, but because of the lack of over-all directional planning at the urban level. These mistakes are exceptionally costly, running into billions of dollars. Recently a Toronto newspaper headline referred to a one billion dollar bungle. Apparently a one billion dollar arterial highway
National Housing Act
program was completed, at which time it was found that it was built in the wrong place. Similar mistakes have been made by almost every other city in the world which has gone through these same growth stages.
I am suggesting that under this urban renewal program and other programs dealing with research, the administration of the Act has the power to go far beyond anything that has been done to date in working with these cities to give that leadership in respect of over-all planning that they must have in looking to the future.
If anything I have said is offensive to any city in Canada, or for that matter in the world, I accept full responsibility. These cities have made a tremendous effort to improve planning over the past 20 or 30 years. However, this final step must still be taken and I suggest to the Minister that in that final step the Federal Government, through the officials who administer Acts such as the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, has a great part to play in carrying forward that initiative which it has developed over the past ten years, in order to move into this new stage of reducing costs for the development of metropolitan areas which has been so sorely lacking in the past.
The next gap to which I should like to refer, and this is perhaps the last one I can deal with during the time at my disposal, relates to the subject of ownership, not only of farms but of homes and resources. One of the great dangers of this modern industrial growth and urban development is related to the recent trend toward rental type accommodation. This type of trend is unsound in a democratic country which prides itself in offering every citizen the opportunity to own a farm, a home or to partake in ownership of resources. I think the obvious answer to this problem has been shown by private enterprise which has made available, in many communities in the world, including Canada, an opportunity for people to build up an equity in apartment blocks. I believe this Act could be easily amended to create that type of incentive to Canadians to acquire ownership or equity in the apartment blocks in which they live.

speechtext: Order, please. Has the hon. Member leave of the Committee to continue beyond his allotted time?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN ADVANCES TO CORPORATION
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN ADVANCES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and Members of the Committee. I think I will

April 27, 1965
National Housing Act
only require three more minutes to complete my remarks.
I would point out that the Act could easily be amended to allow for encouragement in ownership of apartment blocks. In this regard, as well as in respect of ownership of homes, they must give consideration under other legislation to the provision of some relief in the way of taxes on real estate. Several suggestions have been made by my leader and various real estate boards and associations across this country in respect of exemptions of taxes on municipal properties by way of changes in Federal income tax exemptions. Perhaps consideration could be given to placing high on the priority list of exemptions the interest paid on mortgages by individuals purchasing homes. I hope the Minister will give some consideration in this regard in his attempt to develop encouragement in the ownership of homes and apartment blocks. I mention this because of its vital importance.
Mr. Chairman, I have several documents before me including clippings and editorials which touch on this subject, but rather than read them specifically let me say there are many, and I urge the Minister to read them.
The next gap in this proposal is related to the development of isolated areas in Canada. No consideration is given specifically to those developments which take place around mining sites. A good example of this is the difficulty which the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has experienced in respect of the Elliot Lake area. Another example is the new development taking place around Pine Point. Not only are there new mines being developed there, but a new smelter is to be developed very soon. This development will result in a population growth of 10,000 to 20,000. Surely there should be some special type of arrangement made for the financing and developing of areas of this kind, so that if the area is closed down in ten to 40 years an amortization plan can be worked out whereby the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will not be stuck too severely, and the people who move into these areas will not be penalized. This same concept should apply to areas which develop around factory and industrial sites where many hundreds of people are engaged in these operations. We must find solutions to many of these problems so that the equity which is built up by individuals moving into these newly developed areas can be picked up, relieving them of any penalty they would otherwise suffer. The

same thing applies in reverse when factories close down.
It is not clear whether these problems should be solved entirely through amendments to housing legislation or in co-operation with programs of the Department of Industry, but they certainly are worthy of consideration and solution.
The sixth and final gap I see in this legislation relates to increases in land value. At this time people living outside cities may purchase lots for $500, for example. Following growth and development of these areas, these same lots increase in value to as much as $2,000. This means, of course, that late comers to the area must pay $2,000 for these lots before making down payments on homes. It is my belief that this question of increasing land values in areas surrounding cities is of vital concern to Governments. Governments must realize that if we are to have proper metropolitan planning we must know in advance where our cities are going to develop, and obtain these lands so that prospective home owners will not be subjected to tremendously accelerated land values.
I am sorry I do not have sufficient time at my disposal to deal at length with these various insufficiencies of the legislation, but I hope the Minister will give consideration to the gaps which I have outlined. I hope the Government will bring to the attention of the administrators of this Act those areas which I have suggested which could be developed and improved.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN ADVANCES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest to the cheerful and optimistic statement made by the Minister this evening, and it is obvious that if one did not look beyond the surface of his report he would be encouraged. However, if one takes the trouble of scraping below the surface of this report, he will realize the various problems with which the Minister and his Government are confronted, and perhaps realize that the Minister is attempting to make a virtue of a necessity.
As we in this Party have done before, I should like to urge the Prime Minister to make the national housing administration the responsibility of a new Cabinet Minister. In looking at the figures mentioned in this resolution we note that there is to be a $750 million increase, a $200 million increase, a $100 million increase, a $50 million increase and a $2,500 million increase. Clause (e) mentions an increase from $6 billion to $8,500 million which is equivalent to the entire
April 27. 1965

budget proposal by the Minister of Finance. Surely this job is of such a magnitude that it should be the full responsibility of one Minister.
I realize that the present Minister is a very capable man, one of the most capable in the Cabinet. He has become known in certain circles as "Mr. Clean". He has risen from the rather modest position of Minister of Forestry, after getting that Department going, through the Post Office Department, which was put under his charge after the former Minister was promoted to that other place, to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, which was an almost daily embarrassment to the Government. In addition to his responsibility in respect of the administration of the National Housing Act, he has responsibility as the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and as the Minister of two or three other portfolios.
[DOT] (9:00 p.mj
It leads me to believe, Mr. Chairman, that this Government just does not take this particular problem very seriously. They think that this National Housing Act, with all its ramifications, with the fantastic job that it is forced to do today, can be looked after by a Minister who is looking after three or four other departments. I question whether or not the Government have really got their eyes open as to the extent of this problem. I suggest the Prime Minister look around, search amongst his ranks, for a suitable replacement to take the load of these other portfolios off the Minister and put him full time in this particular field. If he cannot find any suitable persons amongst his cohorts, the practice has been long established whereby he can appoint other people.
I am sure, Mr. Chairman, it was only because of the tremendous load of work that has been placed on this Minister that on two successive days he was caught making completely contradictory statements. I might say, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. Member representing the Conservative Party and I seem to be using the same material for our speeches tonight. It seems to me we have brought this House a long way when that happens. However, I must say it is very comforting for us to see this development.
In a recent article in the Globe and Mail, dated December 17 of last year, the Minister stated that nearly 100,000 Canadian families lived in appalling housing conditions which were a disgrace to their communities. This is true, Mr. Chairman, but it is a disgrace to
National Housing Act
more than the communities. This is a responsibility not only of the communities but of the Provinces and of this Federal Government. The disgrace must be shared equally by all three. Having said this, we were very surprised the very next day to see a report in the Globe and Mail in which the Minister was quoted as saying he was opposed to National Housing Act loans for old houses. The reason he gave, and this is in quotation marks was, "lending for improvement of houses is the function of the private part of the economy". Surely, Mr. Chairman, if the Minister was not so loaded down with work, if he had the time to sit down for five minutes and really think about this, he would realize that if this is a job for the private part of the economy they have failed dismally in that job over these years. It is only because of that failure the Government is finally being forced into this field to try to correct the situation.
As I say, on December 17 the Minister appeared to have some grasp of the situation when he said that a comprehensive program of conservation must be undertaken to check blight because demolition is the wrong approach in areas where decline is starting to show. In the face of that statement, how can he turn around the next day and say that lending for the improvement of houses is the function for the private sector of the economy? When the private sector has failed so dismally, how can he hang on to this idea that this is still the solution? How many years of failure does it take before he realizes that this is not the solution and never has been? We have even more double talk.
I sometimes wonder if this apparent confusion, this foggy thinking, is not one of the factors that has contributed to the problem we are now facing when we are finally trying to cope with this problem. In the article of December 18, the same one in which the Minister was quoted as being opposed to National Housing Act loans for old houses, another gentleman, Mr. Donald Guard, planning director of the City of London suggests that some better name be found to replace such terms as urban renewal or redevelopment. The article reads, in part:
He felt such terms put some kind of stigma on an area Residents panic when the label is placed on their district, he said. Mr. Cumming said that if a better word can be suggested, it would be adopted. There may be some persons who object to having their district tagged an urban renewal area, he said, but there are others who simply do not want to face the fact that their area is deteriorating.
You see, Mr. Chairman, this strange feeling that they seem to have, this apprehension

April 27, 1965
National Housing Act
toward an attempt to improve the living conditions of the people. I would say that, to some extent, it is caused by this foggy thinking, this double talk, by statements one way one day and directly opposite the next.
It should be no news that the Minister announced last fall that 100,000 houses needed improvement. If we look back to August 28, 1962, we find the same statement being made then by Mr. E. W. Dempster, who is chairman of the board of the zoning and legislation committee of the Toronto Beal Estate Board. He mentioned then that at least 100,000 houses needed maintenance repairs to avoid costly urban renewal projects by public authorities. Now, we find the Minister saying the same thing some 28 months later. This would appear to me to be nothing more nor less than an admission of complete failure in this field up to date. The Minister admits that there has been no improvement over the last 28 months.
What of the future? To what can we look forward? First of all, I would suggest anyone interested in this subject could do no better than to read a report entitled, "Housing for Canadians". It is a report by Mr. James A. Murray, a professor at the School of Architecture, and was made after a two-year study of public housing which was paid for by the Federal Government and the Ontario Government jointly. This report sets out a certain number of requirements in the housing field and, as I say, it was made after a two year study in this field. It revealed some rather terrifying prospects ahead for this country and for this Government, which has the responsibility. It says that from 1961 to 1981 we are going to need one million subsidized units for low income groups and elderly people. We are going to need another million housing units for the moderate income group, $3,000 to $4,500 a year, people who can pay an economic rent as long as the Government provides the money at cost for capital expenditure. Again, according to this report, in the last 15 years in this field we have only built 42,000 units.
Now, Mr. Chairman, a little simple arithmetic shows us that to meet this problem in the next 15 years we are going to have to do 48 times as well as we did in the last 15. In the Budget Papers presented by the Minister of Finance the other night, page 21, we find the following:
Housing and Social Capital.
Expenditures on new housing in 1964 increased nearly 19 per cent over the previous year. This increase was as large as that realized during the three-year period 1960 to 1963.

[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I would say a 19 per cent improvement on nothing is still not too far from nothing, in the face of the problem set forth by this housing study. It goes on to say:
The chart of population by age groups shows that there are rapidly increasing numbers in the 2024 and 25-29 age groups who normally establish in their own households. In addition, higher incomes in general have permitted "un-doubling" of composite families, with older members and relatives apparently able to afford accommodation of their own. These factors may account for the rising proportion of apartments and multiple units which now amount to over 50 per cent by volume of all new housing construction.
This report goes on to say that people who can afford to pay for housing will need another 2 million units in the same period of time. I am sure the Minister realizes this because he has travelled the country from coast to coast and has met with people interested and concerned in this field. He must realize what a staggering job lies ahead.
So far as the present amendments are concerned, they are only a drop in the bucket, and long overdue. We will support them, in fact we would support them if they were ten times the size they are now, but even then they would not begin to cope with the problem.
Dealing with the amendments we passed last year, which were similar to the present ones, Professor Murray said in his report that-
-to supplement these subsidized housing programs, a large moderate income "full recovery" housing program was also necessary. With this conclusion we are in the fullest agreement. Unfortunately, the recent amendments to the N.H.A. provide no special incentives for launching such a program.
In other words it has not even yet scratched the problem.
I have not got the time to go into greater detail. One matter we have to deal with is the over-all age problem across the country. If we go into regional areas we will find these problems in many towns because in some they need old age units and in other areas there are younger populations in the districts. Possibly we will have time at some future date to deal with that facet of the problem.
One other matter I would like to deal with before my time runs out, is again one that was touched on by the hon. Member for Qu'Appelle but unfortunately, as Conservatives and Liberals have tended to do over the years, when they touch a problem like this they just skip over the top of it and do
April 27, 1965

not get down into the heart of it. This again is one of the millstones that is holding back any sensible, comprehensive housing program across the country, and it is the matter of land speculation.
In the same article of August 28, 1962, Mr. Gavin Henderson, the executive director of the Conservation Council of Ontario, had this to say on land use:
It is largely the widespread speculation in land over the last 15 years or so coupled, of course, with outworn assessment practices, that has been responsible for the appalling waste of some of the best agricultural land in the province. Because land speculation can have such a powerful and detrimental effect on the social and economic welfare of both present and future generations, a revision of our attitude toward this activity is, I suggest, long overdue.
Before he closes this debate I would like the Minister to tell us if the Government has even recognized this problem, let alone taken any steps to try to meet and overcome it. There is certainly nothing in this resolution that we can see to deal with it. There is legislation to come before us under ARDA to try and overcome some of the problems we face in rural areas. We have a trend which is world-wide, not only country-wide, of rural people moving to the cities. They are not prepared for city life and the cities are not prepared to handle them. We have the additional problem, which is becoming more and more prevalent, of the terrific increase in mental illness and crime which accompanies these sprawling slums in our cities.
Once again I would like to read from this report, which is known as the Murray report:
Attention is drawn to the rapid growth of population of Canada, estimated to reach 27 million by 1980, of whom 70-80 per cent will be living in urban areas. "With the inevitable pressure of population, it is problematic that land will continue to be treated as a speculative commodity rather than as a national asset, particularly in the centralized urban areas. When land is assembled by the public purse for central area renewal, it should be leased, not sold; in the redevelopment process, buying once with public funds should be enough."
Before closing I would like to ask what steps the Government is taking to meet these problems I have outlined? Has it really recognized these problems for what they are? I call on the Government to recognize these things and say to it, do not try to hide them; face up to them. As I mentioned earlier, let us take this present Minister, who I am sure commands the confidence of the House, and turn him loose on that problem. Maybe then we can be a lot more proud of what we are doing in this field.
National Housing Act
I would like to close by again quoting from the Murray Report something that is very appropriate to my remarks:
This country is rich; rich in natural and human resources; too rich for ease of conscience while so many Canadians of modest means, or advanced years, must live out their lives in squalid dilapidation and miserable overcrowding, yet surrounded by every sign of extraordinary affluence. The uncertainty, ineffectiveness, inequitable availability and stigma of housing help extended, is nothing less than a national, provincial and municipal disgrace. For those Canadians unable to achieve decent housing it is more than time that 20 years of housing neglect give way to 20 years of housing progress. ... Present and past activities in low income and elderly persons' housing bear absolutely no relationship to any realistic appraisal of the need in Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN ADVANCES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak briefly in support of the resolution. It seems to me the Government is indicating somewhat of a paradoxical position with respect to this measure, because in recent times we found it introducing steps which have been restrictive so far as the construction industry is concerned. On the one hand it imposes an 11 per cent sales tax on building materials, and now it turns around and is making additional moneys available to C.M.H.C. for citizens who desire to build homes. I suppose that the increase in cost occasioned by the sales tax requires that additional funds be provided, and possibly that is one of the reasons for this amendment.
In reading the Speech from the Throne we note the Government indicating an interest in developing a program for the full utilization of our human resources and the elimination of poverty among our people. I believe we would all agree that in the development of our human resources one of the most important factors is the provision of adequate housing.
Even though it is possible to raise a family in poor housing conditions, the full human personality cannot be fully developed for acceptance of its place in society if living surroundings and environment are not conducive to such development. So we should give every encouragement to those who are contemplating building and owning their own homes.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The next paragraph has to do with urban renewal. Here again we recognize a tremendous need. Many citizens and groups of citizens across the country are fully conscious of the need to enter upon major renewal projects. It has been brought to the attention of the authorities and of the public in general that

April 27. 1965
National Housing Act
inadequate housing is a factor contributing to the incidence of social problems of various kinds. In introducing this clause I believe the Minister has recognized the need and is acting in a way which will go some way toward providing solutions.
The resolution also deals with public housing units. I think this is most important. In communities from coast to coast various agencies and organizations are desirous of moving into this field to assist in providing houses for those of our citizens who perhaps are in the low income brackets. They face severe difficulties in obtaining the necessary capital. They try to get co-operation from the various authorities and they do a tremendous job. I think it is essential that the Government should take a definite step forward to provide capital to assist these agencies in such a worth-while project.
Finally there is a reference to university housing projects. Everyone recognizes that with the development of educational facilities in the field of higher education there is need for the adequate housing of the mounting university population. In all these various fields the Federal Government has a responsibility to fulfil and there is an indication in this resolution that the Government recognizes this responsibility and is moving forward.
Once again I emphasize the importance of housing in the over-all social picture of our country. Too often we become obsessed with the economic opportunities which face us as a nation. We become obsessed with the dollars and cents and we forget the necessity of concentrating first of all on our human resources and encouraging the development of human personalities in order to enable our people to enjoy the cultural and spiritual aspects of life as well as its material aspects. Therefore I speak tonight in support of the resolution now before us.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN ADVANCES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it gives me pleasure to join with the other hon. members and say that we give full support to the few minor amendments to the National Housing Act.
I say few minor amendments because we are somewhat amazed to see that the minister, in spite of all his good will-because he is one of the best qualified members of the cabinet-could do no more than touch lightly on the matter. It seems to me that it is a little characteristic of this government to only touch upon matters. In fact, under the

pretence of proposing amendments, the government has touched upon the Income Tax Act, the Senate Act and now, the National Housing Act. I do not know whether that is the main quality of diplomacy in politics. If it is a quality, this government is really expert in those matters.
We had expected a little more substantial amendments dealing especially with construction standards, the conditions of acceptance of such constructions and dealing a little deeper with construction, in urban centres or in rural communities.
Nevertheless, we are happy about the increase in the amounts. It must be noted that it is only a guarantee given by the government to the chartered banks so that the said banks have the assurance that there is no risk for them in granting loans. Indeed, the government will back them up.
Of course, it would be an entirely different story if logically the national bank was used, but the government is not yet ripe for this and it should be given a little time to mature.
The minister said that housing for the aged would be accelerated. This is good news for, in our areas, in our constituencies, especially those in the province of Quebec, we have not benefited too much from this act for the simple reason that we were probably used to build large community homes for the aged, some for men, others for women.
In the province of Quebec we believe in the indissolubility of marriage but, on the other hand, we have always considered up to now that elderly persons had to be segregated before passing away. That is why, in the case of a married couple, the man is placed in one home and the woman in another.
That is what is being done in our areas and I hope that this accelerated program will enable us to accommodate our old people in our own communities and not 125 miles away from our towns.
I earnestly hope that this program will be understood in all parts of the province of Quebec and that one day, in each of our communities, towns and villages, there may be a home for older couples so that in their declining years they may reside in security in their own community.
I wonder if some private contractors could not be given further encouragement. For I have seen contractors building homes for the aged, in some villages, who had to discontinue their building operations because no municipality was sponsoring the housing
April 27, 1965

project. They had invested their own capital to build those homes in some sparsely populated villages where, even now, about 20, 25 or 30 couples could be accomodated in those homes.
There is also a marked improvement in urban centres. We are very happy about the amount that has been voted and we hope that our city councils will realize the taxpayers' needs and especially will take the trouble to study this legislation in order to benefit from it.
I have been very glad indeed a few minutes ago, to hear the statement made by the minister in which he mentioned having toured the provinces to discuss the implementation of these plans with the authorities concerned. I believe that if the minister or someone from his department, would go and meet each township council, in order to advise them and show them the benefits that are available to them through Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation, the government would in this way render a most useful service to the whole population.
It is all very well to pass and to amend legislation; but we realize when travelling through our ridings that 75 per cent of the provisions are completely unknown to our administrators. This is the reason why I said during certain meetings in my riding that it would be imperative that members sit a shorter time in parliament, say six or seven months, and that they take five months to go in every community in their riding and teach the officials the meaning of amendments to legislation, so that all citizens, urban as well as rural, can take advantage of the legislation passed by parliament.
I regret that the minister has not considered introducing an amendment to the act dealing with improvements to older houses. We are now building new towns, neglecting the older parts of communities, precisely because the present terms of loans to owners of old houses are not acceptable.
I would like now, Mr. Chairman, to tell the minister that the conditions we have at the present time because of city zoning- zoning which is practically never discussed- are very embarrassing. I have noticed this anomaly in every town in my riding, and we realize, like the minister, that the owner of an older house who asks for a loan to renovate his house is unable to have one because the city council has not passed a resolution to determine whether this house is in an area designated by them.
National Housing Act
In my opinion, this constitutes a gap in the legislation because, in passing this amendment, we could have offered loans for the renewal of all older houses to those who would like to take advantage of that, without the requirement that this zone must be designated specifically by the city council.
Thus, many loans are lost.
Through personal experience, I may say that in my riding, this year, many loans were lost which could have helped to renovate many old houses which could still have been rebuilt but which are now abandoned due to a lack of a proper amendment.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
We are also somewhat surprised to find that in large cities, the construction of multiple unit buildings or community housing projects is being encouraged by the C.M.H.C. Instead of building 6, 12 or 20 units under the same roof, for instance, a contractor, in order to benefit from the C.M.H.C. legislation, will build multiple unit apartment buildings belonging to the same owner who will be granted such loans.
We are in favour of private enterprise, but we are also in favour of family homes. We would have liked to find in those amendments some encouragement to prompt heads of families to acquire their own homes, instead of living in those community housing projects. That is why we hope the legislation will be further revised soon.
I share the opinion of the previous speaker that when you take charge of a department, Mr. Minister, you seek to make a complete clean-up. You have almost made three complete clean-ups and I am sure that if you keep this department for a while, you will take under consideration as soon as possible the suggestion being made to you.
I frankly admit that we, French Canadians, who like to have our own homes, hate to see families crowded in community housing. This contributes to the loss of our French-Canadian mentality.
We were anxious to see which amendments to the National Housing Act would be introduced tonight. There is nothing in all that. We had hoped to see an amendment to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, because today a farmer cannot get a loan from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to build a house on his farm. Barely 5 per cent of those applications are accepted or likely to be accepted by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It is imperative to amend this legislation so that farmers may also benefit

National Housing Act
from the advantages afforded owners and family heads in urban centres.
Now, only a few words on the extra charges that those who borrow from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have to pay now. Because of a tax increase or for various reasons, the monthly payments are raised. In some cases, those monthly payments are so high that the owner must let his house go. I think that the government would have been wise to introduce an amendment to postpone the payment of these extra charges resulting in those increases until the last instalment has been paid in order not to disrupt the family budget. When somebody builds himself a house with a loan from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, he prepares a budget and plans to pay $55, $60 or $75 a month. But the following year his monthly payments are raised to $85 and $90. Now, you will agree that it becomes impossible for this worker to balance his budget, with the result that, after making sacrifices for four and five years and paying for certain improvements and repairs, including that famous 11 per cent tax, he often has to let his house go.
In my opinion, all those disadvantages are far from encouraging family heads to benefit from opportunities offered by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Nevertheless, we shall support the resolution because it brings us something, even if that is barely 5 to 6 per cent of what was expected from this amendment to the housing act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN ADVANCES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, you will surely forgive me if I seem somewhat parochial this evening but, on second thought, I feel the topic I wish to discuss truly is of national importance.
To walk through the streets of old Quebec is to relive the first chapters of Canada's history. A careful observer cannot fail to notice it, as the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Walker) reminded me no later than last week, on the occasion of his first visit to old Quebec. The narrow streets, the architecture of the churches, houses and monuments, the stones themselves are a testimonial to our history. Here and there, various ugly structures of a more or less recent past mar the harmony and the artistic beauty of the general picture but luckily, old Quebec still retains its charms.
After 300 years the old city still remains a tourist's paradise. For several years now various bodies have been advocating the restoration of old Quebec. To name only a

few, there are the Quebec historic society, the chambers of commerce and the Quebec City council. Lately, the province itself joined in through its historical monuments society and its department of municipal affairs.
The bill that will follow the passing of the resolution now before us will provide, I hope, the financial means to achieve such a restoration.
Last February the general director of the Quebec district chamber of commerce, Mr. Roger Vezina, wrote me a letter which contained the following suggestion:
After agreements have been reached between the federal government and that of a province, the central mortgage and housing corporation could undertake or share with that provincial government or any body designated by that government, in projects for:
(a)	the acquisition, renewal or improvement of historical areas or sites to be devoted, wholly or in part, to housing developments;
(b)	the acquisition, renewal and improvement of historical buildings to be used wholly or partially for housing purposes.
Mr. Vezina added that such legislation was essential to prevent old Quebec from becoming a blighted area and to favour its restoration.
In reply to that suggestion the minister responsible for C.M.H.C. sent me a letter dated March 26, 1965 which I should like to place on record:
I wish to thank you for having forwarded to me the speech which Mr. Roger Vezina, general director of the Quebec chamber of commerce, made before the Societe St. Jean-Baptiste. The senior officials of the Corporation have given careful consideration to that speech, which precisely advocates the adoption of measures to preserve the architectural characteristics of old Quebec.
In replying to Mr. V6zina, you may perhaps underline' that the government of the province of Quebec, to my knowledge, has already taken steps to achieve the aim he supports. As far as the provisions of the National Housing Act, are concerned, no doubt some parts of the old city could rightly take advantage of section 23B, wherein it is provided that the federal government makes grants and loans to a province or a municipality for projects of urban renewal. Such projects do not consist solely in the demolition of dilapidated sections or zones and their replacement with new housing projects; they also provide financial assistance for the renewal of an existing section. Such renewal may comprise improvement of public facilities and services, as well as a program designed to encourage the individuals to renovate their residential properties.
Indeed, the National Housing Act authorizes the corporation to grant loans for this purpose to owners of houses located in urban renewal districts. However. I must point out that although such a financial assistance could very well be granted in the case of some districts of Quebec City, the federal government can take no steps before it has received an official request for assistance

Mr. Chairman, in rising generally to support the amendment put forward this evening by the Minister I should simply like to say that this Party in general, as
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion stated by the Member for Qu'Appelle, has supported this principle of an ownership democracy for some time. This means that it is our feeling that everything possible should be done by the Government to encourage the ownership of homes by Canadians, that everything possible should be done to encourage the ownership of independent businesses by independent businessmen and that everything should be done to encourage good farmers to own good farms. We believe that everything should be done to support the principle of property ownership, because when the state owns too much, in the general sense of that word, a democracy, in the truest sense of that word, becomes imperilled.
On many occasions when I have proposed this principle Members opposite have suggested that I was in fact enunciating a Conservative Party principle of landed gentry ownership in years gone by, or perhaps even in centuries gone by. That is not what I am talking about. I am talking about the desirable notion that everything should be done by the Government to encourage ownership of farms, independent businesses and homes, and in so far as this amendment encourages and projects that principle, like the hon. Member for Qu'Appelle, we support its general purport.
We also recognize that in Canada far too many people in our rural areas are living in abject poverty. While it is good to encourage home ownership we must realize that many Canadians do not have the means of even beginning to own their own homes. It should be recognized that when a married man with a family of four in many instances does not have the means to make a down payment on a home or keep up the monthly or semiannual payments on a C.M.H.C. home, something is drastically wrong and there is a need to attack the more basic problem in this regard.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock.

GRANTS FOR PROVISION OF HOSPITAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I thought it necessary to question the Secretary of State or in his absence the Acting Secretary of State, as to whether or not there has been any restriction placed by the Centennial Commemoration Committee on the granting of Government funds to such memorial projects as extensions to public hospitals or the erection of new hospital buildings. I am personally interested in hospital work, and in making inquiries as to projects approved by the Canadian Government and Provincial Governments with regard to the commemoration of the Centennial of Confederation, I found that in the several hundreds of applications that have already been received and endorsed, Provincially and Federally, there are no direct hospital grants.
A careful inquiry into the list of approved projects and an examination of the names shows that three enterprises in the nature of welfare work have been submitted by Municipalities and approved by the Provincial and Federal Governments concerned. For instance, the good people of Bowness, Alberta, have suggested and the Alberta Government has approved, and the Federal Centennial Commission has verified, that they wish to build an old people's home for senior citizens at Bowness with these triple matching grants. In the Eastern section of Ontario, in the area represented by the Deputy Speaker himself, the United Counties of Glengarry, Stormont and Dundas, have decided to use their centennial commemoration moneys for the erection of an inter-denominational chapel at an old people's home on the outskirts of the City of Cornwall. In Nova Scotia, the Province has decided to use the centennial commemoration grant from the Federal Government of $2.5 million to erect a research and teaching medical school on the campus of Dalhousie University. I do not know of any more worth-while projects for the commemoration of the Centennial of Confederation than the three I have mentioned.
However, as yet, no hospital projects have been brought forward for Federal consideration. I would ask the Secretary of State for Canada if it is because of any roadblocks at the Federal level that hospital projects have not been advanced as suitable memorial projects for the Centenary of Confeder-
[Mr. Grafftey.l
ation? Is it because of some obstacle in the Provincial field? I do not know the answer. On behalf of hospital people from one end of Canada to the other I would ask if the Secretary of State or his representative could advise us as to what the obstacle may be so that steps may be taken to utilize these vast sums of money which have been made available by the Federal Government by way of matching grants so that they can be utilized for hospital purposes. I know of no better way of observing the Centenary of Confederation than by erecting hospital additions or new buildings, so that we who are living can honour those who have gone before us.
I have not had time to check all the hospitals in the Dominion of Canada, but it is amazing to find the number of hospitals that have been erected in the ten Provinces of this country as memorials either to the war dead of the first or second World Wars, or to individuals. Just a quick resume, and I could use up half an hour let alone seven minutes, reveals that in Nova Scotia we have the Fishermen's Memorial Hospital at Lunenburg and the Eastern Shore Memorial Hospital at Sheet Harbour. In New Brunswick we have the Restigouche and Bay Chaleur Soldiers' Memorial Hospital at Campbellton and the Queens-Sunbury West Memorial Hospital at Fredericton Junction. In Prince Edward Island we have the Kings County Memorial Hospital at Montague. In Newfoundland, you have the Western Memorial Hospital at Corner Brook and you have four Grenfell Mission Hospitals in Newfoundland and Labrador, honouring Grenfell. In the Northwest Territories, you have Stanton Yellowknife Hospital at Yellowknife. The list is almost endless.
I say that if we can pay tribute to our war dead and to those who have gone before when we have centres such as the Plummer Memorial Hospital at Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, the Maimonides Hospital in Montreal and the Jeffery Hale's Hospital in Quebec City, surely we could have hospitals across this nation bearing names such as Centennial, or the Centenary of Confederation, so that that name could ring from one side of the country to the other and they would be suitable memorials of the Centenary of Confederation which we will be observing in 1967.
I would sincerely and earnestly ask the Department of the Secretary of State to let us know if there has been some obstacle in the
April 27, 1965

way of making grants available to hospital associations across the country for memorial purposes, or is there an obstacle in some other sphere of influence?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: GRANTS FOR PROVISION OF HOSPITAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the special centenary grants for a major project in each Province are not to be confused with the program of Federal-Provincial grants to assist local centenary projects of a lasting nature.
The Dalhousie Medical School project falls under the former and not the latter program. The special Federal grants to be matched by each Province, amounting to $2.5 million for each Province, are for major projects preferably of a cultural nature, and preferably in the provincial capitals. The Government of Nova Scotia decided that this money should be directed to the Dalhousie Medical School.
The other program, the one to which the hon. Member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) referred, involves a three-way division of costs among the local group, the Province and the Government of Canada. The Centennial Commission has adopted the policy of not considering any local project for a Federal
Business of the House grant unless it comes with the approval of the appropriate provincial authority. In other words, the approval of projects is the concern of the Provinces in the first instance.
No prohibition against hospital projects has been introduced by the Centennial Commission. To my knowledge no hospital projects, other than perhaps the ones the hon. Member has mentioned-if we adopt a broad interpretation of the term-have been brought forward. Hon. Members, of course, know that the Government of Canada already is assisting in the construction of hospitals under another program administered by the Department of National Health and Welfare.
